title: Quantifying Teleportation Overhead in Distributed Unitary Coupled-Cluster Ansätze
authors: Grier M. Jones, Hassan Tariq Shafi, Zixuan Wang, Thomas Trenty, Zachary Vernec, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
abstract: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) has been proposed as a way to scale quantum algorithms for practical applications beyond monolithic quantum processor architectures. Among these applications, quantum chemistry is widely regarded as one of the most promising use cases for quantum computing. In this work, we estimate the distributed-resource requirements of unitary coupled-cluster (UCC) ansätze for quantum chemistry, focusing on unitary coupled-cluster singles and doubles (UCCSD), unitary pair coupled-cluster doubles (UpCCD), and unitary pair coupled-cluster with generalized singles and doubles (UpCCGSD) circuits for hydrogen chains. We focus on a teleportation-based approach to DQC, quantitatively comparing a naive distribution method to the output of the TeleSABRE algorithm. For both approaches, we estimate the cost of handling nonlocal two-qubit gates across a fixed midpoint or quarter-point partition, reporting Bell-pair/classical-communication costs in teleportation. Across Jordan-Wigner and Bravyi-Kitaev, we find that UpCCD with spin-blocked Jordan-Wigner ordering gives the most favorable scaling, while UCCSD incurs substantially larger distributed-resource requirements.
summary: This work quantifies the resource overhead required to run quantum chemistry simulations using Coupled-Cluster methods on distributed quantum hardware. By comparing naive circuit partitioning against the optimized TeleSABRE algorithm, the authors determine that UpCCD is the most resource-efficient ansatz. The findings are critical for understanding the scaling limitations of quantum algorithms on modular quantum processors.
main_problem: The paper estimates the distributed-resource requirements for implementing Unitary Coupled-Cluster (UCC) ansätze in the context of Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC).
main_result: The UpCCD ansatz shows the most favorable scaling for distributed resources, significantly outperforming UCCSD, and the TeleSABRE algorithm substantially reduces required Bell pairs compared to naive distribution methods.
method: The authors compare a naive circuit partitioning approach against the optimized TeleSABRE algorithm to quantify the cost of nonlocal two-qubit gates, reporting costs in Bell pairs and classical communication.
model_or_system: The focus is on quantum chemistry calculations using UCC ansätze (UCCSD, UpCCD, UpCCGSD) applied to hydrogen chains. The resource analysis is performed for two fermionic mappings: Jordan-Wigner and Bravyi-Kitaev.
key_observables: Distributed-resource requirements, quantified by Bell-pair costs and classical communication overhead for nonlocal two-qubit gates.
important_parameters: Hydrogen chain length ($H2n$), and the specific UCC ansatz used (UCCSD, UpCCD, UpCCGSD).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes an implementable gate set including arbitrary-angle rotations, and the resource estimation is limited by memory constraints for larger systems.
figures_summary: Fig. 1 compares two-qubit gates crossing partition boundaries for the three ansätze under naive partitioning. Fig. 2 shows resource estimations (SWAP, Bell pairs) vs. system size for UpCCD and UpCCGSD using TeleSABRE.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of DQC for quantum chemistry, details the resource estimation methodology comparing naive vs. TeleSABRE, presents quantitative results comparing different ansätze and encodings, and concludes with scaling analysis.
why_interesting: It provides concrete, quantitative metrics (Bell pairs, gate counts) for scaling quantum chemistry algorithms onto realistic, distributed hardware architectures, which is crucial for assessing the feasibility of near-term quantum computation.

Fig. 2 presents the resources needed for the UpCCGSD and UpCCD ans¨atze under the JW and BK encodings as a function of hydrogen chain length (H2n) when routing circuits using TeleSABRE. Across both ans¨atze, qubit and Bell-pair counts grow much more slowly than SWAP and gate counts, and the encodings track closely with one another throughout, indicating that TeleSABRE’s routing and layout optimization largely absorbs the encoding-dependent differences observed under naive partitioning. For UpCCD, all four metrics scale similarly across the full range considered.
